key_insight: Simulating near-term QNLP sentence classifiers on a classical state-vector backend is dramatically more expensive than training a matched classical baseline, with only limited and unstable accuracy gains.
engineering_relevance: For practitioners, this paper quantifies the real compute burden of simulator-based QNLP experiments and shows that runtime, not just model accuracy, must be budgeted when evaluating feasibility.
method: Ran a variational quantum classifier for SST-2 sentiment on PennyLane’s state-vector simulator
Swept 27 configurations across training size (N=200, 500, 1000), qubits (4, 6, 8), and circuit depth
Compared against logistic regression on the same PCA-reduced inputs plus an uncompressed TF-IDF baseline
evidence_signal: Across 27 single-seed runs, the VQC beat its matched classical baseline in 6 cases, but after two additional seeds only 1 case retained a positive mean advantage, and paired tests did not confirm a robust gain.
watch_item: The results are tightly scoped to one dataset, ansatz, simulator, and CPU environment, so the findings should be treated as a reproducible cost measurement rather than a general QNLP performance conclusion.
paper_title: What Does It Cost to Simulate a Quantum Sentence Classifier? An Energy and Compute Perspective on Near-Term QNLP
